title: Maharashtra FDA Seizes ₹4.45 Crore in Suspect Food Stock Ahead of Festive Season
excerpt: Officials seized 75 tonnes of branded butter in Ahilyanagar and intercepted paneer and khoya trucked in from Karnataka without cold-chain or labelling, in a 48-hour operation across four districts.
body:
• Maharashtra FDA seized food stock valued at ₹4.45 crore across Ahilyanagar, Pune, Nashik and Buldhana over 48 hours in a pre-festive-season crackdown.
  • The largest haul: 75,356.8 kg of pasteurised cooking butter branded "Madhurama Creamy Delight" worth ₹3.95 crore from a cold storage in Ahilyanagar's MIDC area.
  • In Pune's Budhwar Peth, officials intercepted paneer, khoya and yogurt trucked in from Karnataka's Belagavi and Bagalkot districts without temperature control, batch numbers or expiry dates.
  • 4,627 kg of unlabeled khoya worth ₹11.56 lakh was destroyed at the Hadapsar dumping ground; 69 samples were sent for laboratory testing.

The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration has seized food stock valued at ₹4.45 crore in a 48-hour crackdown across four districts, timed to intercept adulterated and substandard dairy products before they could reach consumers for the festive season. The operation, supervised by FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe, covered Ahilyanagar, Pune, Nashik and Buldhana, and resulted in the seizure of more than 95 tonnes of food items.

The single biggest haul came on September 10, when FDA officials raided the Arihant Cold Storage in the MIDC area of Ahilyanagar and confiscated 75,356.8 kilograms of pasteurised cooking butter branded as "Madhurama Creamy Delight," estimated to be worth ₹3.95 crore. Authorities flagged suspected violations of product quality and labelling regulations, sealed the stock and dispatched samples for laboratory analysis. Further legal action will follow once test results arrive.

Paneer and khoya from across state lines

The following day, acting on a tip-off, FDA teams in Pune stopped two vehicles in the Budhwar Peth area and inspected the premises of M/S KB Agarwal. The consignment — paneer, khoya and yogurt trucked in from Karnataka's Belagavi and Bagalkot regions — was being transported without temperature monitoring equipment, in unsanitary vehicles, and with essential product information such as batch numbers and expiry dates missing entirely.

"The action taken today on khoya and paneer was based on intelligence received from our Commissioner's office, which we had been working on and collecting for the past 10-12 days."

— Nilesh Masare, Assistant Commissioner, FDA Pune Division

In all, the Pune operation yielded 13,360 kg of paneer valued at ₹31.7 lakh and 4,627 kg of khoya valued at ₹11.56 lakh. Another 7,362.5 kg of paneer, khoya and yogurt worth ₹17.15 lakh was placed in cold storage, while 6,081 kg of paneer worth ₹14.55 lakh was seized outright for improper transport conditions. The unlabeled khoya, judged at high risk of spoilage, was destroyed at the Hadapsar dumping ground with the trader's consent. The FDA collected 69 samples in Pune for laboratory testing.

Why the festive season draws adulteration

The timing is deliberate. Demand for milk products — paneer, khoya, curd, ghee and butter — surges during Ganeshotsav, Navratri and Diwali, and that seasonal spike has long made the festival calendar the peak season for food adulteration in Maharashtra. Traders who place bulk orders with suppliers across state borders often move perishable dairy through unregulated transporters, where cold-chain gaps turn a quality problem into a public-health risk.

Masare said the Pune consignment had been ordered by roughly 30 to 35 traders in the city and district. All invoices and bills are in hand, he told ANI, and a full investigation into the supply chain will proceed alongside the laboratory analysis. Officials have said strict action will follow against anyone in the chain if the seized products are declared unsafe or adulterated.

Part of a wider enforcement push

The seizure adds to a string of recent Maharashtra FDA actions against dairy fraud, including the state's one-year ban on analogue paneer and licence suspensions for establishments caught serving it. The pattern is consistent: intelligence-led raids, sample collection, cold-storage sealing and destruction of stock judged unsafe on the spot.

For consumers, the FDA's message is unchanged: check packaging for batch numbers, manufacturing and expiry dates, and buy dairy from vendors with visible cold-chain handling — especially during the festival weeks when sweets and paneer move in the largest volumes of the year.

What's next

Laboratory reports on the 69 samples will determine the next phase of enforcement, including prosecutions under the Food Safety and Standards Act. With Navratri and Diwali still ahead, the FDA has signalled that inspections will continue through the season, and officials have asked the public to report suspected adulteration on the FDA's toll-free helpline, 1800-222-365.
nri_angle: Diaspora families ordering sweets and dairy from Indian suppliers during the festival season face the same adulteration risks, and should buy from licensed vendors with proper labelling and cold-chain handling.
author: Diaspora Desk
